turn_text: (upbeat music) - Hi, I'm Arlene McIntyre, Creative Director at Ventura Design, and you're listening to "Shut the Front Door," a lighthearted podcast that will bring you through the front door and into the homes of influential and interesting people. John McCallgan is a multi-award-winning producer and director who started his career in the mid-70s at RTE, going on to become its head of entertainment. He then went on to become a head of weekend entertainment on TVAM in London. John is also the director of Riverdance, heartbeat of home, a numerous other stage and TV productions. With his wife and business partner, Moia Daugherty, together with Bill Whelan, they created Riverdance, initially as an interval act the 1994 Eurovision contest. And then just a year later, they had produced a full two-hour show which they launched in Dublin. Riverdance went on to become the global Irish dance phenomenon that we all know, love and are so proud of. John is also an accomplished photographer and an avid supporter of human rights and became the first ambassador for Chocra, with whom he produced the acclaimed photography exhibition and TV documentary, This is Palestine. John has four children, a daughter and three sons, including two sons with Moia. He is also a grandfather to his beloved Lord. John, thank you so much for joining us today and shut the front door.
assumption_text: The host believes that creating a 'home' involves emotional resonance and lasting personal significance.

I was born in Straban in County, Turon at the end of World War II, and my father had been in the army and he moved or got a job in firms in a leather factory and year after year, my mother had three kids. I was the eldest, so I was left behind in Straban with my granny and I lived in a road called Newtown, Mon, Canada, which is a road of terraced houses that looks a bit like Carnation Street. And that was the first sort of four years of my life was spent there and I didn't really see my mother until I was about four. And I made strange with her when they brought me back. But I have fond memories and I have a photograph of me standing on the house of the terraced house, pulling a little wooden horse. And my granny was a rather formidable woman and she read quite a bit. And if I was messing about behind her, she would comment on what I was doing and I would say, "How do you know what I'm doing?" And she said, "I have eyes in the back of my head." So I kept the back of her head and see where these eyes were. But that was the first four years and I enjoyed it. And I had an aunt there that was very close to me. My father's sister, Antibriety, was there. She was very kind and very good to me and she was a sort of surrogate mother and I had a close relationship with her for the rest of my life. And I saw her on a regular basis and we all loved her. She passed away about 20 years ago. But I made it down to ferns and we lived in a bungalow on a farm, belonging to a wonderful family called O'Tooles. So it was a nice bungalow, three miles away from the school that I went to school. It was a lovely country school. There were three teachers and one of the teachers who taught me all of those years ago is still alive. To us she was a Miss Baker, but she became Mrs. Consulate. And I saw her last year when I went down. She's 94 or something in good health. She was quite a formidable strict teacher, but she was a very good teacher. And she was also our music teacher. So we had a choir that she had put together and I sang in that choir and we went into NS Coursy to the cathedral and we sang there and she prepared us for our confirmation and so on. So it was a lovely school surrounded by beautiful rolling hills and you could hear all the agricultural activity tractors and dogs barking. And I really loved it. And I think it imbued in me living there and all the experience of the seasons and seeing the seasons imbued in me a lot of nature and the sons and the country, Patrick and Lewis who have unfortunately passed away. They were really good to me and they took me out on the tractor and they took me out at night time when they were going out to look at the lambs with the tilly lamp. And those of you may not want tilly lamp is, but it was a lamp that you put in the carasene and you pumped it and it gave off very strong light. So season in season out, I was involved with the farmers in what they were doing here in my first money thinning turnips down on your knees with the Hessian sack going along a drill and taking out the turnips. And then Mr. Tule, an extraordinary woman who would come out at lunchtime with the big Hessian sack again with bottles of tea, quite often in leukazade bottles with that stippled neck and the tea would be have the sugar and the milk and everything we'd stand and then big door stops of sandwiches. So you'd sit in the sunshine. I always thought it was sunny. And with the other working man and you'd have your lunch and the hedge in the field. And I loved my teacher in school, a man called Mr. Lynch and he was in charge of the amateur dramatic society and then a score fee. He was also an amateur magician and historian. So I was really fortunate to have him as a teacher. So he made history so interesting and he made us re-plays and read Shakespeare and then he would do some magic tricks. So he was fantastic. It was a mixed school. And the girl who brought me to school, a girl called Josephino Tule. She was about five or six years older than me, but she took me to school when I was four, four and a half. And she was a great friend. She was also very interested in theater. And when she went to secondary school, she was one of the leaders in the, in Tullow in the musical society in the school. So the first show I ever saw live on stage was "H.M.S. Pinaform." And she was in that, and I was really fascinated by that. So it probably was one of the first things that sparked my love of theater and live
